en: The Sūtra on Samajja Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Wu-period Indian Śramaṇa Zhu Lüyan.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
There were one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and five hundred bodhisattvas present, along with kings, commoners, and various devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits beyond counting.

At that time, there was a king of the country of Nala named Pindola; he did not believe in the Buddha-dharma but favored non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas), daily providing meals within his palace for more than ten thousand nirgranthas.
The King of Dhanaka was habitually arrogant and considered his own wisdom to be peerless; he bound his abdomen with iron plates, constantly fearing that his wisdom might burst forth from his belly.
The king, wishing to take a wife for his crown prince, immediately questioned his surrounding ministers:
"Is there anyone in the world whose wisdom is equal to mine?
If there is such a person, I wish to marry their daughter to my son."

The minister, having received the king’s command, immediately traveled throughout the kingdom searching for such a person; finding no one at all who matched the king’s description, and knowing himself that there was none in the kingdom, he dispatched messengers once more to other countries to seek a wise man and his wife.
At that time, the messenger received the king’s instructions and proceeded to the kingdom of Śrāvastī. Upon arrival, the messenger asked the people of the country:
"Is there anyone in this land who is a virtuous man skilled in the Way?"
The person replied, "There is.
The messenger said:
"What is your family name and given name?
The person replied,
"My given name is Buddha."
The messenger asked,
"Does the Buddha perhaps have a daughter?
The man replied:
"The Buddha is a man of the Way; he has no women.
The messenger asked, "Who else is next?"
He replied, "There is another man named Anāthapiṇḍika, a great sage who is virtuous and fond of the Way; he has a beautiful daughter, the foremost in the kingdom.
The messenger said:
"What makes him the foremost?

The people of the kingdom replied, "He once requested with Prince Jeta that they purchase eighty *qǐng* of garden land to offer to the Buddha. Furthermore, he used elephants to transport several hundred thousand *bì* of gold to pay for the land; he did not covet these precious treasures, but thought only of performing good deeds."
Upon hearing the words of the people in the kingdom, the messenger was greatly rejoiced; knowing that he had obtained news, he immediately returned to his own country and said to the king:
"In the city of Śrāvastī, there is a virtuous and excellent man who is deeply devoted to the Way, named Ānanda-bhadrika."

When the King of Nala heard the messenger’s words, he immediately wrote a letter and dispatched the crown prince along with his ministers and officials. They prepared their carriages and loaded them with precious treasures, traveling together to the kingdom of Śrāvastī. They halted the prince outside the city and sent a messenger into the city to the residence of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At that time, the gatekeeper went inside and informed Ānanda-Bhadrika:
"An envoy has arrived outside.
Ānanda-Bhadrika immediately went out to meet him at the gate; seeing that the envoy was as black and hideous as a ghost, Ānanda-Bhadrika was greatly startled and said:
"What kind of person are you?
He replied immediately,
"I am a messenger from the King of Dhanakaṭaka."
Anāthapiṇḍika said,
"What do you seek by coming here?
The messenger replied:

"I have come to proclaim the Buddha's teachings. Although King Nala does not see me in person, he regards me with distant affection and respect. People who travel back and forth constantly sing praises of your immeasurable merit; hearing that you are virtuous and deeply devoted to the Way, and that you have a daughter, I have come wishing to seek your daughter for the Crown Prince. The King has also sent his own letter to inform you."

Anāthapiṇḍika was about to revile him, but he restrained himself and said nothing; instead, he called him forward to sit with him, exchanged greetings and conversation, and the messenger then showed him the letter.
Having finished reading the scripture, Ānanda-bhadrika replied to the messenger, saying:
"I have a superior to whom I must report this; if he permits me, I shall return to inform you of the news."
He then detained the messenger and sat down. Ānanda-bhṛtya went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself before the Buddha, withdrew to kneel with palms joined, and said to the Buddha:

"Now the king of the land of Dhanaka has sent a messenger to my house; his appearance is as dark as a ghost, and he says that he wishes to seek my daughter Samajī for the crown prince of the king. What should I do now?"
The Buddha said,
"Give it to him.
Anāthapiṇḍika said:
"The messenger is black as a ghost; what must his king and crown prince be like?

Furthermore, I have heard from the Buddha that the King of Dantapura serves only the Nirgranthas, who go naked without clothing and are ugly and black in appearance—could they not terrify my daughter?"
The Buddha said, “No;
give it to him. You should know that by this causal condition, Samagama shall deliver eighty thousand people in the land of the naked.”
Ānanda-bhadrika did not dare to question the Buddha further; harboring resentment in his heart, he immediately returned home and said to the messenger:
"Since you have come from afar at the king's command to seek my daughter, that is most excellent; I shall grant her to you."
Having heard Ānanda-Bhāradvāja’s words, the messenger immediately returned to the city and went to where the prince was; he then accompanied the prince back to Ānanda-Bhāradvāja’s residence.

He immediately descended from his carriage and bestowed gold, silver, and wedding gifts upon Ānanda-Bhṛtya. Then, together with him, he invited guests and entertained them with food and drink for seven days. When the period was concluded, Ānanda-Bhṛtya sent Triśaṅku away, providing him with male and female servants, clothing, and precious jewels in countless quantities. The prince then took Triśaṅku with him and returned to his own country.

At that time, when King Nanda saw his daughter-in-law returning home, he was filled with great joy. He immediately invited his teacher, Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, along with twelve thousand disciples, to enter the palace for a meal; King Nanda and his queen, as well as the crown prince, all personally attended to the serving of the food.
At that time, Samajiva was summoned to come out, intending to have him serve the food and join in paying respects to the various teachers.

When Samajiva reached the third gate, he saw from afar all the Nirgranthas sitting in rows, naked and without any clothing or coverings. Samajiva was immediately struck with great alarm; thinking they were no different from dogs or other beasts, he covered his face with both hands, spat at them from a distance, and immediately returned to his room, refusing to come out again.
All the Nirgranthas were filled with indignation toward Samaja and immediately addressed the king, saying:
"From where did you obtain this deluded and inauspicious man to enter the royal palace?"
“Send them away immediately! If you do not send them away, they shall bring ruin upon the kingdom.
The Nirgranthas refused to eat further and were about to rise and depart, whereupon the king apologized to the masters:
“I shall have the Great Master send them away; tomorrow they shall no longer appear within the palace.”
When the various Nirgranthas had finished eating their meal, they departed.

On that very day, the Prince went in person to where Samaja was; however, at that time Samaja was greatly enraged and ordered his maidservant to close the door. This continued for four or five days, during which the Prince did not dare to go again.
The lady immediately asked the prince, "For what reason do you not go?
The prince remained silent and did not speak; the lady understood this from his silence and went herself to the place where Triśaṅku was.
"I have taken you as my daughter-in-law; you should now serve my son. Why do you insult him?
Samajja replied, "Madam, the teachers your son serves and the people of this country are all no different from dogs or beasts."
Upon hearing this, the lady was deeply ashamed and immediately returned to inform the king, saying: "Great King!

You yourself consider your wisdom in the Way to be peerless, and since there is no one in the kingdom who meets with Your Majesty's approval, you have instead exhausted your ministers by seeking a bride eight thousand *li* away."
"Now this woman, without any fear or hesitation, has humiliated my son and furthermore insulted me to my face, comparing me to dogs and beasts.
Upon hearing the lady’s words, the king immediately went in person to where Samajika was.
At that time, Samajja was greatly arrogant and refused to come out to pay homage to the king.
The king then asked Samajja from afar:
"I traveled eight thousand li to marry you because of your virtue and goodness."
"If the messenger has already insulted my teacher, and now you further insult the lady and the prince to his face,
how could this not be unacceptable? Samajja replied,
"Indeed it is."
“The Great King’s teacher, his consort, the crown prince, and the people of the kingdom are all no different from dogs or beasts.
The king was immediately startled and said,
“She is but a young girl!”

Now that you have humiliated me in this way, I fear my wisdom will burst forth from my belly; I shall encase my abdomen in iron plates! Daily I provide meals for more than ten thousand practitioners of the Way—who could possibly equal me?
"Why do you now confront and revile one another face-to-face?

Samajja replied, "The teachers served by the people within the king's realm are always without clothing; they stand naked before one another. What kind of Way could there possibly be in such a practice?"
Even if they possessed the Way, they would not be worthy of honor, let alone if they lacked it.
Great King!
Although you feed more than ten thousand such people every day, they are all those whom I do not respect; they are always spittle and contempt.
At that time, King Nanda, being utterly exhausted, thought to himself:
"With whom should I deliberate on this matter?
He then went in person to where the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra was, prostrated before his teacher, and said:

"I took a wife for myself from the city of Śrāvastī; recently she has behaved improperly, having already brought disgrace upon the Great Master, and now she again insults me, my lady, and the Prince with arrogance, comparing us to dogs and beasts."
"Although she is my wife, she does not serve me with the propriety due to a wife; what should I do now?
The teacher told the king:
"Go back and ask her again, saying:"
"What are the objects of worship for the people in your country compared to those of the people in my own country?"—such were his words.
"When the King goes there, do not become angry; inquire gently, and he will surely speak."
The king immediately accepted the instruction and, following his teacher’s words, went to Samajja and asked:
“What is it that the people in your country practice that makes them superior to the people in my own country?”

Samajjha said: "In my country, the people serve those who are most honored; both men and women wear garments; the noble and the humble travel on separate paths; and their bodies do not come into contact with one another."

There currently exist Buddhas, both great and small, who instruct tens of billions of people, causing them all to attain the path of nirvana that transcends the world; they enter fire unburnt and enter water unsunken.

He is able to encompass the three thousandfold great chiliocosm with its suns and moons and its twelve trillion worlds; he manifests transformations, entering the Avīci hell and emerging from the space between atoms; he knows all matters of the future, the past, and the present; his body possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; his virtue and wisdom are fully realized; and the devas, kings, emperors, and common people gather together to bow their heads and pay him homage.
When King [Nanda] heard Samajaka’s words, he immediately leaped for joy with great delight.
At that time, King Nanda said to Samajaka:
“Is it possible for me to see the Buddha whom you serve?”
Samajja said, "I can request him for the Great King from afar; he can be brought here.
The King said:
"Excellent! Since we are eight thousand li apart, how should we invite the Buddha? Samajja said:
“There is no need for Your Majesty to send someone to invite me; you should simply offer incense with sincere devotion from afar.
The Buddha’s supernormal powers perceive what is in people's minds, and the King’s consort and the Crown Prince shall both follow behind me.”
Samajja immediately ascended the high platform, adjusted his robes, and facing the city of Śrāvastī, knelt and burned incense. Placing his head and face upon the ground, he prostrated and said:

"The King of Dhanakaṭaka does not know that there is a Buddha in the world. For the sake of all the people and out of compassion for those who suffer, I pray that the Buddha, together with the community of bhikṣus, will deign to honor us by coming to the residence of the King of Dhanakaṭaka tomorrow morning for a meal."
As soon as he had finished speaking, the fragrant smoke reached the place where the Buddha was; it circled the Buddha three times and transformed above him into a fragrant canopy.
At that time, the Buddha was preaching the Dharma for countless thousands of people. Then Ānanda came forward, knelt with his hands joined in *añjali*, and said to the Buddha:
"What kind of spiritual resonance is this, that it has manifested in such a way?"
“I pray that the Buddha will explain its meaning.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The King of Dantapura and the King of Samajya shall invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus tomorrow morning.”
Samajja possessed a sincere heart; wishing to cause all the people of the kingdom of Nāṇa to abandon false views and turn toward the Right Path, he brought this incense here to invite the Buddha.
At that time, he immediately addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana and commanded the community of bhikṣus: "Tomorrow morning, you shall go to the kingdom of Nanda to the residence of Samajika for a meal.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Mahāmaudgalyāyana proclaimed it to the bhikṣus:
"Tomorrow we shall attend the invitation; do not go elsewhere."

Thereupon, Samajjha ordered the king, the queen, the crown prince, and all the court ladies to observe the fast and purify themselves; they burned incense, spread out seats, and prepared a full array of food and drink.
Samajja, knowing that the Buddha was about to arrive, stayed with the king, the queen, the crown prince, the palace ladies, and the various Nirgranthas in the central courtyard.
Samajja addressed the king, the queen, and the crown prince:
"All follow behind me; now the Arhats shall arrive first, and the Buddha will be the very last."
"You all must not be alarmed or terrified; follow whatever I do.
Thereupon, Samajja again knelt down on his knees, burned incense, and said:
"The meal is prepared; I pray that the Buddha will partake at this time."
The Buddha, knowing what Samagama was thinking in his mind, immediately addressed the bhikṣus:
"Today we shall go to the kingdom of Nanda for a meal; each of you should manifest transformations through the Way according to your own mastery."

The bhikṣus immediately accepted the instruction; among them were those who manifested as dragons, tigers, phoenixes, peacocks, oxen, doves, and pigeons, as well as a hundred kinds of birds, owls, and beasts forming a lattice-canopy. All the members of the Saṃgha sat within it, each appearing different from the others.

At that time, the Buddha sat himself within a lion-canopied pavilion, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, five hundred bodhisattvas, and various devas, asuras, gandharvas, and nāgas; they traveled through the air by means of supernatural power.

Upon arriving at the country of Durdharṣa, the Buddha immediately emitted a brilliant light, and heaven and earth shook violently. All the *arhats* and *bodhisattvas* manifested various supernatural transformations and descended first; when the people of Durdharṣa saw these manifestations, they were all struck with great terror.
The king asked Samajja,
"Is this the Buddha? He replied:
"It is not the Buddha," Samajja told the king.
"Do not be afraid; these are his disciples."
The Buddha was at the very rear; his body was endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

In an instant, the Buddha descended together with them from above, preceded by Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings. The various devas played lutes and performed music as an offering to delight the Buddha.

Samavarta, together with the king, the queen, and the crown prince, immediately took flowers and incense to welcome the Buddha; they prostrated before him and then escorted him into the palace, where he took his seat.

The bodhisattvas and arhats all sat down in order of seniority; Samudra then had the king, his queen, and the crown prince go forward to provide water for washing and set out the food and utensils. A great multitude of people from the kingdom came to watch, so the king ordered his ministers to close the palace gates.
When the people saw the King shut the palace gates, they became greatly incensed with the King and each took an axe, intending to break down the gates.
The Buddha knew this from afar and said:
"The purpose of my teachings and transformations is solely to lead all beings to do good. Now that the people of the kingdom have come to see me, the King has instead shut his palace gates."

At that time, the Buddha, wishing for all people to behold him, caused the palace gates and walls to transform entirely into the color of crystal, so that the interior and exterior could see one another. The people of the kingdom who saw the Buddha, as well as the various bodhisattvas and arhats, were all filled with great joy.

At that time, there was an arhat of the Buddha named Piṇḍola who happened to be sitting on a mountain and had forgotten that he was in the country of Zhinan. Piṇḍola had been sitting there for a long time; he then wished to sew a garment with a needle and thread, so he pricked the ground with his needle, and the thread became attached to the garment.

At that time, after the Buddha had finished responding to the King’s difficult questions and was seated within the palace, Piṇḍola immediately traveled by means of his supernatural power to the kingdom of Nanda; the mountain then followed behind Piṇḍola.
At that time, there was a woman in the kingdom who was pregnant; seeing the mountain approaching, pitch black, she feared it would fall upon her, and in great terror, she immediately miscarried.
The Buddha, knowing this from afar, immediately commanded Mahāmaudgalyāyana to fly forth by means of his supernormal powers to welcome him and inquire:
"Piṇḍola! What is your name?"
Pindola immediately looked back and saw the mountain; he seized it with his hand and hurled it back to its original place, eight thousand li away.
At that moment, Pindola arrived before the Buddha, paid homage, and withdrew to sit.
The Buddha told Piṇḍola:
"I teach all people in the world so that they may all cross over into liberation. Now you have both missed the appointed time and killed a person.
Human life is most precious; such an act is not what my Way approves."
"From this day forward, you must no longer follow me for meals or attend my assemblies.
If you remain here, you shall only enter parinirvāṇa after Maitreya Buddha appears."

Having heard the Buddha speak thus, Piṇḍola remained silent, filled with sorrow and remorse. When he had finished eating, he rose and went forward to pay his respects; then, together with the various bodhisattvas and arhats, he took his leave and entered the mountains.
At that time, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, the royal preceptor of the kingdom of Vesālī, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Shall we not compete in the Way?
If I am defeated, I shall throw myself into a well."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! There is no need for further words. If you lose to me three times in questioning, you shall be cast into a well."
The Nirgrantha Jñātiputra said, "Very well!
The Buddha then asked:
"What about when reciting the sūtras?
Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta replied,
"When I recite the sūtras, I crawl along."
"To crawl on all fours is the way of a dog; dogs indeed crawl on all fours.

When Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was thus surpassed by the Buddha, his disciples all became enraged. They reviled Caṅkī for having correctly explained this matter, and they all returned in a fit of rage to their teacher’s dwelling. They seized their teacher, intending to throw him into a well; the teacher was then greatly terrified and, pressing both hands against the ground, refused to enter the well.
The Buddha said, "Leave it be.

At that moment, a great fire spontaneously erupted from the middle courtyard, its flames ascending as far as the seventh Brahma Heaven. Within that fire, there were naturally lotus flowers with a thousand petals, and upon each flower sat five hundred Brahmās, all of whom joined their palms, knelt on one knee, and questioned the Buddha:
“By offering food to what kind of person does one obtain much merit?
By offering food to what kind of person does one obtain little merit?
The Buddha replied to the Brahmā:
“Suppose, for example, one were to scatter five kinds of seeds into a fire;
would they grow? Brahmā replied, “They would not.”
The Buddha said, "The various Nirgranthas whom King Nanda has fed in the past and present are like five grains of rice cast into fire; they will never grow again.
But by feeding me and the bodhisattvas and arhats today, you shall obtain immeasurable merit."
For example, if a person has fertile soil and excellent seeds, and the heavens send timely rain, why worry that they will not grow?
Now, the Buddha is the field of merit for all people; according to what one sows, one will surely obtain their wish.

Foolish people delight in instructing others to become non-Buddhists; when such people’s lives end, they shall all fall into the Tai Shan Hell, where they undergo extreme suffering. There will be no time for repentance once it is too late, and while the predecessor remains there without having escaped, the successor again instructs them to do the same. The people of this world are so foolish that they merely deceive and manipulate one another; therefore, they do not know the True Path.
If there is a wise person, they should study the Right Path; that path is neither born, nor does it age, nor is it ill, nor does it die—it is the Great Way of Nirvana.
Among all the ninety-six kinds of paths existing in the world, none equal the Buddha’s Way.
The Buddha said:

"If one were to take the branches of all the trees and the feathers of all the birds in a single world-system to fashion brushes for writing the Buddha’s sutras, those tree branches and bird feathers might all be exhausted, but the Buddha’s wisdom could never be exhausted.

Even if one were to grind ink as large as Mount Sumeru and dip a brush in the waters of the four oceans, that ink from Mount Sumeru and those waters of the four oceans might all be exhausted, but the Buddha’s wisdom would ultimately never be exhausted."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, five hundred Brahmās raised their voices at that moment and said:
“Excellent! It is truly as the Buddha has spoken.”
Thereupon, the five hundred Brahmā deities suddenly vanished.

At that time, three hundred members of King Nanda’s retinue, twelve hundred court ladies, and five hundred ministers, having witnessed the Buddha’s miraculous transformations, all leaped for joy and, with great delight, resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, two thousand brahmins immediately shaved off their hair and beards and became bhikṣus; they all attained the path of arhatship at that very moment.

Twelve thousand nirgranthas were likewise liberated at that very moment: among them, some attained the path of srotāpanna, some attained the path of sakṛdāgāmin, and some attained the path of anāgāmin.
Furthermore, there were sixty-four thousand commoners within the kingdom who all placed their faith in the Buddha-dharma;
they immediately received the five precepts and became upāsakas.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, he and the bodhisattvas and arhats simultaneously manifested their supernatural powers and flew away.

At that time, the King of Nalaṅga, his consort, the crown prince, the ministers, and the people were all filled with great joy; they all prostrated themselves, placing their heads upon the ground, and paid homage to the Buddha from afar.
The Sūtra on Samajja Spoken by the Buddha
